questions.question: A Streptococcus pyogenes isolate is tested as resistant to penicillin.

parts.text: What are 5 things you can do to verify this result?

questions.model_answer: Ways to verify apparent penicillin resistance in S. pyogenes (essentially universally penicillin-susceptible - resistance has never been confirmed): (1) Repeat identification to confirm the isolate is truly Streptococcus pyogenes (group A strep) and not a misidentified viridans/other streptococcus (2) Repeat susceptibility testing using a validated reference method (e.g., broth microdilution or Etest per CLSI) (3) Confirm proper inoculum, incubation conditions, and media used for testing (4) Send the isolate to a reference/public health laboratory for confirmatory testing (5) Rule out laboratory/clerical error (specimen mix-up) by correlating with the original culture and patient's clinical course.

questions.question: Young person who comes in with hip pain out of proportion and hypotension. You suspect necrotizing fasciitis

parts.text: How can this diagnosis be confirmed?
Devise an empiric regimen for the person
Intra-operative sample gram stain shows gram positive cocci in chains, what if any isolation requirements are required?
You learn he was in contact with his mom who is anaphylactic to penicillin. List antibiotics from 2 different classes that can be used for prophylaxis (assuming susceptibility)

questions.model_answer:
a) Necrotizing fasciitis is confirmed by immediate surgical exploration - the gold standard: gray/dishwater fluid, non-bleeding and non-contracting fascia/muscle, and easy separation of fascia from subcutaneous tissue with blunt dissection (positive finger test); frozen-section biopsy and Gram stain of exudate can support intraoperative diagnosis. Adjuncts such as CT/MRI (soft tissue gas or fascial edema) or the LRINEC score can raise suspicion preoperatively but should never delay surgical exploration.
b) Empiric regimen: vancomycin (or linezolid, to cover MRSA) PLUS piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem (e.g., meropenem, to cover streptococci, Enterobacteriaceae, and anaerobes) PLUS clindamycin (to suppress toxin/exotoxin production if group A Streptococcus is implicated).
c) Gram-positive cocci in chains on intraoperative Gram stain suggests group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes); given this, droplet precautions should be added to contact precautions until the patient has received at least 24 hours of effective antimicrobial therapy.
d) For post-exposure prophylaxis of a close contact in a patient with penicillin anaphylaxis, two agents from different classes: clindamycin (lincosamide) and azithromycin (macrolide) - avoiding all beta-lactams, including cephalosporins, given the anaphylactic history.

questions.question: Healthy guy has necrotizing fasciitis of the upper arm

parts.text: How to confirm diagnosis
What is an empiric antibiotic regimen
Gram stain shows gram positive cocci in chains, describe precautions required
Wife has anaphylaxis to Penicillin, list 2 agents from different classes that can be used for post-exposure prophylaxis

cohort_answer.text: Confirm diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis from surgical intervention - rapidly progressive, pain out of proportion, dishwater fluid appearance when fascia is entered surgically. The fascia at time of direct visual examination is swollen and dull gray with stringy areas of necrosis; a thin, brownish exudate may be present. Empiric regimen: Piperacillin-Tazobactam, Vancomycin, Clindamycin. Precautions: Contact and droplet until on appropriate therapy for 24 hours. Post-exposure prophylaxis: Azithromycin 500mg PO daily x5/7; Clindamycin 300mg PO TID x10/7; PCN dosing 250mg PO QID x10/7

parts.text: Wife has anaphylaxis to Penicillin, list 2 agents from different classes that can be used for post-exposure prophylaxis

questions.model_answer: For post-exposure prophylaxis of invasive GAS in a penicillin-anaphylactic contact, two agents from different classes: (1) A macrolide (e.g., azithromycin) or clindamycin (lincosamide) (2) A first-generation cephalosporin is avoided given anaphylaxis; alternative options include clindamycin plus a fluoroquinolone-class or cephalosporin-class agent if not cross-reactive - practically, clindamycin and azithromycin are the two most accepted non-beta-lactam options from different classes.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific contact prophylaxis regimens follow PHAC/IDSA invasive GAS post-exposure guidance.

questions.question: An isolate of group A streptococcus is resistant to erythromycin.

parts.text: List TWO mechanisms of resistance to this antibiotic.
The isolate is susceptible to clindamycin on phenotypic testing. What additional test should be performed in the local microbiology laboratory?

questions.model_answer:
a) Two mechanisms of macrolide resistance in GAS: (1) Target-site modification via ribosomal methylation (erm gene, e.g., ermB/ermTR) causing the MLSb phenotype (cross-resistance to macrolides, lincosamides, and streptogramin B) (2) Efflux pump-mediated resistance (mef gene) causing the M phenotype (macrolide resistance only, with preserved clindamycin susceptibility).
b) With erythromycin resistance but clindamycin susceptibility on routine testing, perform a D-test (double-disk diffusion test) to detect inducible clindamycin resistance (inducible MLSb phenotype) before using clindamycin clinically.

questions.question: Regarding streptococcus toxic shock syndrome

parts.text: In addition to hypotension, what are TWO (of 6) other criteria for toxic shock syndrome
What are the criteria for contacts to get prophylaxis?
What prophylaxis would you offer as first line (just antibiotic, not doses)
What prophylaxis would you offer if the patient had SJS to penicillin?
What are TWO advantages of linezolid over clindamycin in toxic shock syndrome?

questions.model_answer:
a) Two other criteria (of 6) besides hypotension for strep TSS: (1) renal impairment (creatinine ≥177 µmol/L or ≥2x baseline) (2) coagulopathy (platelets ≤100,000/mm³ or DIC) - other options include liver involvement, ARDS, generalized erythematous macular rash (may desquamate), and soft tissue necrosis (necrotizing fasciitis/myositis/gangrene).
b) Criteria for contact prophylaxis: household contacts with substantial exposure time (e.g., ≥4 hours/day or ≥20 hours/week in the week before onset) to a confirmed invasive GAS case, particularly those at higher risk of severe disease (age ≥65, diabetes, chronic illness, HIV, varicella in the past 2 weeks, IV drug use).
c) First-line prophylaxis antibiotic: a first-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cephalexin).
d) If the patient had SJS to penicillin (severe/anaphylactic beta-lactam allergy): use clindamycin or a macrolide (azithromycin) instead of a cephalosporin.
e) Two advantages of linezolid over clindamycin in strep TSS: (1) No risk of inducible or constitutive MLSb resistance (unlike clindamycin, which can fail with inducible-resistant strains) (2) Excellent oral bioavailability (~100%), allowing reliable oral step-down therapy.

questions.question: What antibiotic prophylaxis would you recommend (if any):

parts.text: A. Repeated isolation of GAS from a throat swab
B. Man who shared a cigarette with a patient who subsequently develops meningococcal meningitis 5 days later
C. Contact of a patient with Strep pneumo pneumonia

cohort_answer.text:
Chronic GAS carrier (asymptomatic) = no. Ppx offered if part of institutional outbreak, outbreaks of acute rheumatic fever/post strep GN, infections recurring in household/close contacts. Cephalexin 250mg QID x10 days, Amox 500mg BID x10 days, Erythromycin 250mg QID x10 days (if ceph allergic), Penicillin 300mg VK QID x10 days (alt)
Incubation period of Meningococcus is 1-10 days, usually less than 4 days. IPAC uses 7 days before illness onset as relevant duration. Exposure to oral secretions confers risk, no duration needed, therefore yes. Would give ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1
Prophylaxis not routinely recommended. Would consider age and medical condition: appropriate pneumococcal vaccination

questions.question:
Q11 (2004 AM)
Group A Streptococcal toxic shock

parts.text: A) Name the toxin associated with it

cohort_answer.text: SpeA, SpeC, SpeG to M; SSA – Streptococcal superantigen; SMEZn – streptococcal mitogenic exotoxin Zn

questions.question:
Q11 (2004 AM)
Group A Streptococcal toxic shock

parts.text: B) Describe the effects of the toxin (ie. Superantigen)

cohort_answer.text: Pyrogenic exotoxins (scarlatina toxins, erythrotoxins) cause fever, enhance susceptibility to endotoxin, suppress IgM antibody synthesis, and act as superantigens. Can stimulate T-cell responses by binding to both MHC class II APC's and to the T-cell receptor itself. Causes induction of monocyte cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6), and lymphokines (TNF-beta, IL-2, and interferon-gamma)

questions.question:
Q11 (2004 AM)
Group A Streptococcal toxic shock

parts.text: C) List the antibiotics that are used and give rationale for their use

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin - all strains of GAS susceptible to penicillin; less effective during stationary growth phase (Eagle effect). Clindamycin - suppresses exotoxin and protein M production at ribosome; suppresses cytokine production by human mononuclear cells (also: Penicillin - bactericidal effect; Clindamycin - bacteriostatic anti-toxinic effect + inoculum effect)

questions.question:
Q12 (2004 PM)
Group A Streptococcal toxic shock

parts.text: A) Mechanism of toxic shock syndrome

cohort_answer.text: Production of superantigens causing massive cytokine release, leading to significant hypotension via profound vasodilation and capillary leak

questions.question:
Q12 (2004 PM)
Group A Streptococcal toxic shock

parts.text: B) Strep toxic shock – virulence factor, mechanism of action of virulence factor

cohort_answer.text: SpeA, SpeC, SpeG to M; SSA; SMEZn. Pyogenic exotoxins. MOA: indiscriminately binds to both MHC class II antigen presenting cells and to the T cell receptor to cause profound cytokine release

questions.question: Unstable patient with clinical picture of necrotizing fasciitis, swab of clinical sample is positive for GPC in chains.

parts.text: Empiric Abx
What are two other treatments that must be considered?
What is the underlying virulence factor
Wife asks whether she is at risk for invasive GAS compared to the general population. What do you tell her?

cohort_answer.text: Empiric: PipTazo + Vanco + Clindamycin (awaiting speciation); once GAS confirmed: Pen G + Clinda. Other treatments: Surgical debridement for source control, IVIG (consider for streptococcal TSS), fluid resuscitation. Virulence factor: M protein (major somatic virulence factor of GAS, antiphagocytic via alternate complement pathway inhibition). Risk to contacts: risk of subsequent invasive GAS disease among household contacts is roughly 20-fold (Mandell's: 66/100,000 vs 3.5/100,000 in general population); some sources cite 200-2000 fold higher risk than general population

questions.question: Strep pyogenes testing for erythromycin resistance.

parts.text: Name 2 mechanisms (1)
It demonstrates clindamycin susceptibility. What test do you have to do to confirm this (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: Mechanisms: Alteration in the ribosomal target site or efflux pumps (Mandell's) - mefA efflux pump (specific to strep, other names for staph); MLSB (macrolide lincosamide streptogramin B) resistance from ribosomal methylation altering ribosomal binding site, can be constitutive or inducible (induced by erythromycin exposure making resistant to clindamycin via inducible erm gene). Test: Do inducible clindamycin resistance testing (D-zone test) - only used for Staph species, S. pneumoniae, and beta-hemolytic streptococci; only performed in isolates erythromycin resistant and clindamycin susceptible; detects erm gene-mediated resistance (ribosomal methylation); confers MLSB phenotype

questions.question: Fill the table for mechanisms of macrolide resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae. Indicate if also resistant to clindamycin (lincosamide).

parts.text: For strep pneumo and GAS, for each mechanism (alter the macrolide binding site on bacterial ribosome; active macrolide efflux pumps) state the mechanism of resistance, gene involved, and clindamycin resistance (yes/no). [Table also references Staph aureus, but corresponding rows were not preserved in extracted text]

questions.model_answer: For Streptococcus pneumoniae (and Streptococcus pyogenes/GAS): (1) Ribosomal target site modification - mechanism: erm gene product methylates an adenine residue on the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit, reducing binding of macrolides, lincosamides, and streptogramin B (MLSb phenotype); gene involved: ermB (S. pneumoniae) / ermA, ermB (GAS); clindamycin resistance: YES (cross-resistant, as clindamycin binds the same ribosomal site). (2) Active macrolide efflux pump - mechanism: an efflux pump exports macrolides out of the cell, conferring resistance to 14- and 15-membered macrolides only (not lincosamides); gene involved: mefA/mefE (S. pneumoniae) / mefA (GAS); clindamycin resistance: NO (lincosamides are not substrates of the mef efflux pump).
questions.beyond_mandell: Standard clinical microbiology teaching on macrolide resistance mechanisms (erm vs mef); this content could not be located in the Mandell 'Parechoviruses' chapter that was linked to this question - the pagefile provided (ch179.txt, Chapter 173 Parechoviruses) does not cover macrolide resistance, so no Mandell page citation is given. This mismatch between question content and linked chapter should be flagged for review.

questions.question: Purulent cellulitis in homeless individual.

parts.text: Name the two most likely pathogens to cause this
Tells you he cut it in sea water concerning for vibrio vulnificus, what empiric oral agent could cover all 3 organisms?
He gets allergy to that agent, design two regimens with a single daily IV and/or BID oral that could be used instead of above.
Name 5 organisms (genus and species) of acute water SSTI.

questions.model_answer:
a) The two most likely pathogens causing purulent cellulitis in this population: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus).
b) Doxycycline is a reasonable single empiric oral agent providing activity against MRSA, streptococci, and Vibrio vulnificus.
c) Two alternative regimens (single daily-dose IV and/or twice-daily oral, maximum two drugs each): Regimen 1 - ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV once daily (covers Streptococcus and Vibrio) plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole PO twice daily (covers MRSA). Regimen 2 - ertapenem 1 g IV once daily (covers Streptococcus, Vibrio, and other gram-negatives) plus linezolid PO/IV 600 mg twice daily (covers MRSA and Streptococcus).
d) Five organisms causing acute water-associated skin/soft tissue infection: Vibrio vulnificus, Aeromonas hydrophila, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, and Edwardsiella tarda.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific antibiotic dosing regimens reflect standard clinical practice/IDSA SSTI guideline principles beyond the exact Mandell text.

questions.question: Person has a fluctuant mass in his neck with erythema, swelling and tenderness. For the following scenarios, name the most common pathogen and the most appropriate specimen and microbiologic test.

parts.text: Recently ate steak tartar
Immigrant from Vietnam, also has cough and weight loss over few weeks
Bit by a rabbit on the shoulder
Inflamed tonsils with exudate

cohort_answer.text: Steak tartar: Toxoplasma gondii. Blood serology acute and convalescent. Immigrant from Vietnam: Tuberculosis adenitis - fine needle aspiration or excisional biopsy for AFB and mycobacterial culture. Rabbit bite: Francisella tularensis, blood serology at time of presentation and 2-4 weeks after. Inflamed tonsils: Strep pyogenes. Pharyngeal culture. Parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal collection may need to be drained and can be cultured
